\chapter{Introducing Yourself}
\label{ch:introductions}

\section[me]{me — your first pronoun, and a \emph{real} English twin}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-me}



\begin{quote}
A tiny word doing big work. \emph{me} is your first \textbf{pronoun} — and unlike \emph{hola}, its English look-alike is the real thing: a true cousin, not a coincidence.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-e} — one clean syllable, \emph{meh} (the \emph{e} of \emph{bed}).
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{me} — \textquotedblleft{}me / myself.\textquotedblright{} Root: Latin \textbf{me} (the object form of \emph{ego}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}).

Here's the satisfying part: English \textbf{me} is a \textbf{genuine cousin}, not a false friend. Spanish \emph{me} comes from Latin \emph{me}; English \emph{me} comes from Proto-Germanic — but both trace back to the \emph{same} ancient ancestor (the Proto-Indo-European root \emph{me-}, \textquotedblleft{}me\textquotedblright{}). So do English \textbf{my} and \textbf{mine}. This is the opposite of the \emph{hola}/\emph{hello} trap you saw earlier: here the resemblance is real, and you can lean on it hard. Spanish \emph{me} = English \emph{me}, all the way down.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what a pronoun is}]
A \textbf{pronoun} is a stand-in word that points to a person or thing without naming them — \emph{I, you, he, me, it}. \emph{me} specifically is an \textbf{object} pronoun: it marks the person the action lands on (\textquotedblleft{}call \emph{me}\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}give \emph{me}\textquotedblright{}). In Spanish it usually sits \textbf{right before the verb} — you'll see it next lesson in \emph{me llamo}, literally \textquotedblleft{}myself I-call.\textquotedblright{} For now, just hold \emph{me} = \textquotedblleft{}me / myself.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}me\textquotedblright{} — \emph{meh}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}me\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}me\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}mine\textquotedblright{} — all one family
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is Spanish \emph{me} a true cousin of English \emph{me}, or a coincidence like \emph{hola}/\emph{hello}? (A true cousin — both from the same ancient root.) What part of speech is it? (A pronoun.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[llamo]{llamo — \textquotedblleft{}I call,\textquotedblright{} from a root that shouts}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-llamar}



\begin{quote}
The verb inside \textquotedblleft{}my name is.\textquotedblright{} On its own it means \textquotedblleft{}to call\textquotedblright{} — and its Latin root literally means \emph{to shout}, which is why it echoes through a whole family of English words.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item me — you'll bolt \emph{me} onto \emph{llamo} next lesson.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ll-y} — \textbf{ll} sounds like English \textbf{y}: \emph{llamo} is \emph{YA-mo}, not \emph{LA-mo}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{llamo} — \textquotedblleft{}I call.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form (the infinitive) is \textbf{llamar}, \textquotedblleft{}to call.\textquotedblright{} Root: Latin \textbf{clamare}, \textquotedblleft{}to cry out, to shout.\textquotedblright{} That \emph{clam-} shouts all through English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ex\textbf{claim}, ex\textbf{clam}ation — \emph{ex-} (\textquotedblleft{}out\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{clamare}: to shout \textbf{out}.
  \item pro\textbf{claim}, pro\textbf{clam}ation — \emph{pro-} (\textquotedblleft{}forth\textquotedblright{}): to call \textbf{forth}.
  \item ac\textbf{claim} — \emph{ad-} (\textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{}): to shout praise toward.
  \item \textbf{claim}, re\textbf{claim}, dis\textbf{claim}; and \textbf{clam}or, borrowed whole.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{A sound-pattern to bank:} Latin \emph{cl-} became Spanish \emph{ll-}. \emph{clamare} $\to$ \emph{llamar}. It happened repeatedly: \emph{clavem} $\to$ \emph{llave} (\textquotedblleft{}key\textquotedblright{}), \emph{flamma} $\to$ \emph{llama} (\textquotedblleft{}flame\textquotedblright{}), \emph{plovere} $\to$ \emph{llover} (\textquotedblleft{}to rain\textquotedblright{}). A Spanish word starting \emph{ll-} is very often a Latin \emph{cl-}/\emph{fl-}/\emph{pl-} word in disguise — and its English cousin usually kept the original cluster (\emph{clamor}, \emph{flame}, \emph{pluvial}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}llamo\textquotedblright{} — \emph{YA-mo}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}llamo\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}exclaim\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}proclaim\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}clamor\textquotedblright{} — the shouting root
  \item \textquotedblleft{}llamar\textquotedblright{} (to call), \textquotedblleft{}llave\textquotedblright{} (key) — both from Latin \emph{cl-}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the root \emph{clamare} mean? (To shout / cry out.) Latin \emph{cl-} becomes which two letters in Spanish? (\emph{ll-} — \emph{clamare $\to$ llamar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[me llamo]{me llamo — \textquotedblleft{}I call myself\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-me-llamo}



\begin{quote}
Snap the last two lessons together — \emph{me} + \emph{llamo} — and you can introduce yourself. But notice Spanish doesn't say \textquotedblleft{}my name is\textquotedblright{} at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item me · llamo
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{me llamo} = \textbf{me} (\textquotedblleft{}myself\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{llamo} (\textquotedblleft{}I call\textquotedblright{}) = literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I call myself.\textquotedblright{}} Then the name: \emph{Me llamo Susana} — \textquotedblleft{}I call myself Susan.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: reflexive verbs}]
When the action loops back onto the person doing it — you call \emph{yourself} — the verb is \textbf{reflexive}, and Spanish marks it with that little pronoun in front: \emph{me} (\textquotedblleft{}myself\textquotedblright{}). \emph{llamo} alone is \textquotedblleft{}I call {[}someone else{]}\textquotedblright{}; \emph{me llamo} is \textquotedblleft{}I call \textbf{myself}.\textquotedblright{} English can do this (\textquotedblleft{}I call myself Sam\textquotedblright{}) but usually doesn't bother, flattening it to \textquotedblleft{}my name is.\textquotedblright{} Spanish keeps the reflexive loop visible.

This matters because the pronoun \textbf{changes with the person}: \emph{me} llamo (I call myself) $\to$ \emph{te} llamas (you-informal call yourself) $\to$ \emph{se} llama (he/she/you-formal calls himself). You'll meet \emph{te} and \emph{se} in a few lessons; for now, lock in \emph{me llamo} for yourself.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Spanish presents your name not as a thing you \emph{have} (\textquotedblleft{}my name is\textquotedblright{}) but as what you \emph{do} — what you call yourself. It's subtly more active, and it's the completely standard, neutral way to introduce yourself.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}me llamo\textquotedblright{} + your own name
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hola, me llamo \_\_\_\textquotedblright{} — greeting + introduction
  \item what does \emph{me llamo} literally mean, word for word?
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Literally, what is \emph{me llamo}? (\textquotedblleft{}I call myself.\textquotedblright{}) What makes it reflexive? (The \emph{me} — the action loops back on you.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tú / usted]{tú and usted — two words for \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} and why you must choose}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-tu-usted}



\begin{quote}
English has one word for \textquotedblleft{}you.\textquotedblright{} Spanish has two, and picking the wrong one can send the wrong social signal. This lesson gives you both and shows the everyday choice. The remarkable history of \emph{usted} comes next.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words}
\textbf{tú} — \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} \textbf{informal}. For friends, family, children, peers, anyone you're on easy terms with.

\begin{quote}
Root: Latin \textbf{tū}. This is a \textbf{true cousin} of English \textbf{thou} — the word English used to have for exactly this job, the intimate \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} (\emph{thou/thee/thy}), before it faded out around 400 years ago. Both \emph{tú} and \emph{thou} come straight from the same ancient root (\emph{tu-}). So Spanish still uses, every day, the pronoun English quietly retired.
\end{quote}

\textbf{usted} — \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} \textbf{formal}. For strangers, elders, officials, customers, anyone you're showing respect or keeping distance with.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the choice English lost}]
Both are \textbf{subject pronouns} — the \textquotedblleft{}doer\textquotedblright{} word, like \emph{yo} (\textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}). But they carry a second layer English dropped when \emph{thou} died: \textbf{social register}. Choosing \emph{tú} vs. \emph{usted} tells the listener how you see the relationship — close or respectful. English \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} is one-size-fits-all; a Spanish speaker must decide every time.

One structural surprise, because it explains the next lessons: \textbf{usted takes \emph{he/she} verb forms}, not the informal \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} forms. That's why \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{} formally is \emph{¿cómo \textbf{se llama} usted?} (the \emph{se llama} you'd use for \textquotedblleft{}he calls himself\textquotedblright{}) and not \emph{te llamas}. The next micro-lesson explains the history behind that third-person pattern.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tú\textquotedblright{} — for a close friend
  \item \textquotedblleft{}usted\textquotedblright{} — for someone you'd address respectfully
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tú\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}thou\textquotedblright{} — the retired twin
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which is formal, \emph{tú} or \emph{usted}? (\emph{usted}.) What English pronoun is the lost twin of \emph{tú}? (\emph{Thou}.) Which verb pattern does \emph{usted} take? (The same form used with \textquotedblleft{}he\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}she.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vuestra merced to usted]{\emph{vuestra merced} $\to$ \emph{usted} — respect compressed into one word}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-usted-origin}



\begin{quote}
You use \emph{usted} for respectful \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} and it takes the same verb form as \textquotedblleft{}he\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}she.\textquotedblright{} That surprising grammar preserves the word's history.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item tú / usted — the informal and formal choices.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{usted} wore down from \textbf{vuestra merced}, \textquotedblleft{}your grace\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}your mercy.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Vuestra} comes from Latin \emph{vestra}, \textquotedblleft{}your.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Merced} comes from Latin \emph{merces, mercedem}, \textquotedblleft{}wages, reward, favor.\textquotedblright{}

The \emph{merc-} root links \textbf{mercy}, \textbf{mercenary}, \textbf{commerce}, \textbf{merchant}, and \textbf{merchandise}. A respectful title was repeated so often that two words compressed into one pronoun. Its older abbreviation \textbf{Vd.} still preserves the \emph{v} of \emph{vuestra}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
A title like \textquotedblleft{}your grace\textquotedblright{} refers to a respected person in the third person. That is why modern \emph{usted} still takes the he/she verb form even while it means \textquotedblleft{}you.\textquotedblright{} The social history remains visible in the grammar.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two-word title that became \emph{usted}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}usted\textquotedblright{} followed by \textquotedblleft{}mercy\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}merchant\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{merc-} family
  \item which verb pattern \emph{usted} takes
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{vuestra merced} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Your grace\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}your mercy.\textquotedblright{}) Why does \emph{usted} take the he/she verb form? (It began as a third-person title.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cómo]{cómo — \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} your first question word}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-como}



\begin{quote}
To ask someone's name or how they are, you need this word first. \emph{cómo} — \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{} — and it carries a little word for \textquotedblleft{}manner\textquotedblright{} you already own in English.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{inverted-marks} — Spanish questions open with an upside-down \textbf{¿} so you see the question coming: \emph{¿cómo…?}
  \item \texttt{accent-mark} — the accent on \textbf{ó} marks the stress \emph{and} flags it as a question word (see below): \emph{CÓ-mo}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cómo} — \textquotedblleft{}how.\textquotedblright{} Root: Latin \textbf{quomodo} — a fused little phrase, \emph{quo modo}, \textquotedblleft{}in what \textbf{manner}.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{The two halves, and their English cousins:}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{modo} (\textquotedblleft{}manner, measure\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ English \textbf{mode}, \textbf{mod}al, \textbf{model}, \textbf{mod}erate, \textbf{mod}ify, com\textbf{mod}ity.
  \item \emph{quo} (\textquotedblleft{}in what\textquotedblright{}) is the Latin question-stem \textbf{qu-} — the seed of almost every Spanish question word (see the family below).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{How \emph{quomodo} became \emph{cómo} — the wearing-down.} Spanish didn't borrow \emph{cómo} ready-made; it \emph{eroded} out of \emph{quomodo} over centuries of everyday speech. The final \emph{-do} fell off and the middle collapsed:

\begin{quote}
\emph{quomodo} $\to$ \emph{quomo} $\to$ \textbf{como}
\end{quote}

The \emph{qu-} (a \emph{kw} sound) flattened to a plain \emph{k} (written \emph{c} before \emph{o}). What's left is \emph{quomodo} worn smooth — the way a pebble loses its edges in a river. The same erosion gave Italian \emph{come}, Portuguese \emph{como}, French \emph{comme}. The accent in \emph{cómo} is the one late addition: Spanish stamps it on to mark the question (vs. accent-less \emph{como}, \textquotedblleft{}like / as\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the accent that marks a question}]
Watch the accent mark do real work. \textbf{cómo} (with the accent) = \textquotedblleft{}how?\textquotedblright{}, the question word. \textbf{como} (no accent) = \textquotedblleft{}like / as,\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}I eat.\textquotedblright{} Same letters, and the written accent is the \emph{only} thing telling you it's a question:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{¿\textbf{Cómo} estás?} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{How} are you?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{\textbf{Como} tú.} — \textquotedblleft{}Like you.\textquotedblright{} / \emph{Yo \textbf{como}.} — \textquotedblleft{}I eat.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

English has no such marker — it relies on word order and context. Spanish puts a visible flag on the question word. Every question word you'll learn (\emph{qué, dónde, cuándo, quién…}) carries this accent for the same reason.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿cómo?\textquotedblright{} — with question intonation
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cómo\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}mode\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}model\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{modo} root
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Walk the erosion: \emph{quomodo} $\to$ ? $\to$ \emph{cómo} (\emph{quomo} $\to$ \emph{como}, then the question-accent). What changes when the accent disappears? (\emph{como} is no longer the question word \textquotedblleft{}how.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[qu-]{The \emph{qu-} question family — one ancient pattern, many clues}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-familia-qu}



\begin{quote}
You traced \emph{cómo} back to Latin \emph{quomodo}. Focus now on its first piece, \emph{qu-}, without trying to use a whole set of new question words yet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item cómo — \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \emph{quomodo}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin used a recurring \emph{qu-} stem in questions. Spanish preserves that family, although centuries of sound change gave the modern forms different shapes:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish clue} & \textbf{$\leftarrow$ Latin} & \textbf{future meaning} \\
\midrule
\emph{qué} & \emph{quid} & what \\
\emph{quién} & \emph{quem} & who \\
\emph{cuál} & \emph{qualis} & which \\
\emph{cuándo} & \emph{quando} & when \\
\emph{cuánto} & \emph{quantus} & how much \\
\textbf{cómo} & \emph{quomodo} & how \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

These are previews, not vocabulary to produce today. For now, use the family only as an etymological clue: a question form beginning \emph{qu-} or \emph{cu-} may continue the same Latin pattern. \emph{Dónde}, \textquotedblleft{}where,\textquotedblright{} is an exception from Latin \emph{de unde}, \textquotedblleft{}from where.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the Latin source of \emph{cómo}
  \item the recurring Latin question stem
  \item whether the table is today's production list or a preview
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which old stem connects \emph{qué, quién, cuándo,} and \emph{cómo}? (\emph{qu-}.) Which word in the preview is the exception? (\emph{Dónde}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[se llama]{se llama — the reflexive that fits \emph{usted}}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-se-llama}



\begin{quote}
You can say \emph{me llamo} (\textquotedblleft{}I call myself\textquotedblright{}). To ask someone \emph{else} their name — especially formally, with \emph{usted} — you need the version that loops back on \emph{them}: \emph{se llama}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item me llamo — the reflexive \textquotedblleft{}I call myself.\textquotedblright{}
  \item tú / usted — and the key fact that \emph{usted} takes \emph{he/she} verb forms.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{se llama} = \textbf{se} (\textquotedblleft{}himself / herself / yourself-formal\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{llama} (\textquotedblleft{}calls\textquotedblright{}). So \emph{se llama} = \textquotedblleft{}he/she calls himself,\textquotedblright{} or — because \emph{usted} uses third-person forms — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{you} (formal) call yourself.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{se} — the reflexive pronoun for the third person (and for \emph{usted}). Root: Latin \textbf{sē} (\textquotedblleft{}himself, herself, itself\textquotedblright{}). That same \emph{se-} — carrying the sense of \textquotedblleft{}self / apart / aside\textquotedblright{} — is bolted onto a shelf of English words:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{se}cede — \emph{se} + \emph{cedere} (\textquotedblleft{}go apart\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{se}clude, \textbf{se}gregate (\textquotedblleft{}apart from the flock\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{se}parate.
  \item \textbf{se}duce — \emph{se} + \emph{ducere} (\textquotedblleft{}lead aside\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{se}cure — \emph{se} + \emph{cura} (\textquotedblleft{}free from care\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{se}cret (\textquotedblleft{}set apart\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}

Every one is something turned in on itself or set apart — the same idea as a reflexive looping the action back on the doer.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the reflexive pronoun changes with the person}]
The verb \emph{llamar} stays, but the little reflexive word in front shifts to match \emph{who} is doing the calling:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{me} llamo — \emph{I} call myself
  \item \textbf{te} llamas — \emph{you (informal, tú)} call yourself
  \item \textbf{se} llama — \emph{he / she / you (formal, usted)} calls himself/yourself
\end{itemize}

Three persons, three pronouns: \emph{me / te / se}. That \emph{se} is exactly why the formal \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{} is \emph{¿cómo \textbf{se} llama usted?} — \emph{usted}, born from \textquotedblleft{}your grace,\textquotedblright{} politely takes the \emph{he/she} shape.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}se llama\textquotedblright{} — \emph{seh YA-ma}
  \item the set — \textquotedblleft{}me llamo, te llamas, se llama\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}se\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}secede\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}seclude\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}separate\textquotedblright{} — the set-apart root
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which reflexive goes with \emph{usted} — \emph{te} or \emph{se}? (\emph{se} — because \emph{usted} takes third-person forms.) What's the \textquotedblleft{}self/apart\textquotedblright{} root inside \emph{secede} and \emph{separate}? (Latin \emph{se-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[¿cómo se llama usted?]{¿cómo se llama usted? — assembling the question, and answering it}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-como-se-llama}



\begin{quote}
Everything you built this chapter clicks into one sentence: how to ask a stranger their name, and how to answer back. This is your first real two-way exchange.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item cómo · se llama · usted
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{¿Cómo se llama usted?} = \emph{cómo} (\textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{se llama} (\textquotedblleft{}do you-formal call yourself\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{usted} (\textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} formal).

Literally: \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}How do you call yourself?\textquotedblright{}} Spanish asks \emph{how}, not \emph{what}, for a name — you're asking by what name a person goes, the manner they're called.

\textbf{The informal version}, for a friend, swaps the reflexive and drops the formal pronoun: \textbf{¿Cómo te llamas?} (\emph{te llamas}, from \emph{tú}). Same question, two registers — exactly the \emph{tú}/\emph{usted} choice from earlier, now live in a real sentence:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item To a stranger, an elder, a customer $\to$ \emph{¿Cómo se llama usted?}
  \item To a friend, a child, a peer $\to$ \emph{¿Cómo te llamas?}
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{How to answer}
You already have the answer from the \emph{me llamo} lesson: \textbf{Me llamo \_\_\_.}

\begin{quote}
— ¿Cómo se llama usted? — \textbf{Me llamo David.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ask a stranger their name — \emph{¿cómo se llama usted?}
  \item ask a friend the same — \emph{¿cómo te llamas?}
  \item the whole mini-exchange — ask, then answer with \emph{me llamo \_\_\_}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Formal vs. informal \textquotedblleft{}what's your name\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{¿Cómo se llama usted?} / \emph{¿Cómo te llamas?}) Does Spanish literally ask \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{} is your name? (\textquotedblleft{}How\textquotedblright{} — \emph{cómo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mucho]{mucho — \textquotedblleft{}much,\textquotedblright{} and a sound-change you've already seen}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-mucho}



\begin{quote}
One more word before \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you.\textquotedblright{} \emph{mucho} — \textquotedblleft{}much, a lot\textquotedblright{} — and it hides the same Latin-to-Spanish sound trick you spotted in \emph{noche}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{soft-c} — the \textbf{ch} is the \emph{ch} of \emph{church}: \emph{MOO-cho}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mucho} — \textquotedblleft{}much, a lot.\textquotedblright{} Root: Latin \textbf{multus} (\textquotedblleft{}much, many\textquotedblright{}). The English cousins keep the original \emph{-lt-}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{mult}iple, \textbf{mult}itude, \textbf{mult}iply, \textbf{mult}i-purpose, \textbf{mult}imedia.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The sound-change, again:} Latin \emph{multum} $\to$ Spanish \emph{mucho}. The Latin \textbf{-lt-} softened into Spanish \textbf{-ch-} — the very same move as \emph{noctem $\to$ noche} (\emph{-ct- $\to$ -ch-}, as in the \emph{noche} lesson). Spanish has a habit of melting these consonant clusters into \emph{ch}. So a Spanish \emph{-ch-} word very often points back to a Latin \emph{-ct-} or \emph{-lt-} root — and the English cousin usually preserves it (\emph{noct}urnal, \emph{mult}iple).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mucho\textquotedblright{} — \emph{MOO-cho}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mucho\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}multiple\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}multitude\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{mult-} family
  \item \textquotedblleft{}noche\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}mucho\textquotedblright{} — two words, same \emph{-ch-} from a melted Latin cluster
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{mucho} comes from Latin \emph{multus} — what English words keep the \emph{-lt-}? (multiple, multitude, multiply.) What Latin cluster melted into the \emph{-ch-}? (\emph{-lt-}, like \emph{-ct-} did in \emph{noche}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mucho gusto]{gusto $\to$ mucho gusto — \textquotedblleft{}much pleasure\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-gusto}



\begin{quote}
The line you say when you shake someone's hand. First the noun \emph{gusto}, then snap \emph{mucho} onto it, and you've got it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item mucho — \textquotedblleft{}much,\textquotedblright{} about to modify \emph{gusto}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el gusto} (masculine) — \textquotedblleft{}taste; pleasure, liking.\textquotedblright{} Root: Latin \textbf{gustus} (\textquotedblleft{}a tasting, a taste\textquotedblright{}). The English cousins:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{gust}atory — to do with the sense of taste.
  \item dis\textbf{gust} — \emph{dis-} (\textquotedblleft{}not, opposite\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{gust}: literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{dis}taste.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{gusto} — borrowed whole into English, meaning zest, relish, enjoyment.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
False friend to flag: a \emph{gust} of wind is \textbf{not} related — that one's from Old Norse \emph{gustr}. Same spelling, different root. Resemblance isn't proof.
\end{quote}

\textbf{mucho gusto} = \emph{mucho} (\textquotedblleft{}much\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{gusto} (\textquotedblleft{}pleasure\textquotedblright{}) = literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}much pleasure\textquotedblright{}} — short for \textquotedblleft{}it's a great pleasure {[}to meet you{]}.\textquotedblright{} \emph{gusto} is masculine (\emph{el gusto}), and \emph{mucho} is in its plain masculine form to match it: another quiet piece of the agreement you've been building.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Spanish greets a new acquaintance by naming the \emph{pleasure} of it — \textquotedblleft{}much pleasure\textquotedblright{} — where English names the \emph{person} (\textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet \textbf{you}\textquotedblright{}). The phrase works by itself, so this first exchange needs no extra reply formula.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gusto\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}gusto\textquotedblright{} (English), \textquotedblleft{}disgust\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}gustatory\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mucho gusto\textquotedblright{} — on meeting someone
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{mucho gusto} literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Much pleasure.\textquotedblright{}) Is \emph{el gusto} masculine or feminine? (Masculine.) And the English cousin of \emph{gusto} built from \emph{dis-}? (\emph{Disgust} — \textquotedblleft{}distaste.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — introducing yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C03-practice}



\begin{quote}
Ten lessons of atoms now assemble into a real conversation. No new words — just the exchange, run both formally and informally until the \emph{tú} / \emph{usted} choice is automatic.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\textbf{Formal} (a stranger, an elder, a customer):

\begin{quote}
— Buenos días. Me llamo Susana. \textbf{¿Cómo se llama usted?} — Me llamo David. \textbf{Mucho gusto.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Informal} (a friend, a peer): only two words change, and they're the ones that carry the whole social difference:

\begin{quote}
— ¡Hola! Me llamo Susana. \textbf{¿Cómo te llamas?} — Me llamo David. Mucho gusto.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{me llamo} — introduce yourself (\textquotedblleft{}I call myself\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{tú / usted} — the informal vs. formal \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{why} (the retired \emph{thou}; \emph{usted} from \textquotedblleft{}your grace\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{¿cómo te llamas? / ¿cómo se llama usted?} — ask a name, in either register, the pronoun (\emph{te} / \emph{se}) tracking the choice.
  \item \textbf{mucho gusto} — \textquotedblleft{}much pleasure,\textquotedblright{} pleased to meet you.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the full \emph{formal} exchange, both parts
  \item the same exchange \emph{informally} — catch yourself on \emph{se llama} $\to$ \emph{te llamas}
  \item for a police officer, then your best friend — which \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} for each, and why?
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Run the formal version start to finish without stopping.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two words change between the formal and informal introduction? (\emph{se llama usted} $\to$ \emph{te llamas}.) Next chapter, you will learn how to ask how someone is doing.
\end{tcolorbox}
